seoDescription: Discover why developers are moving from Express.js to modern alternatives like Bun and Hono. This guide demonstrates how to build a high-performance web server using the ultra-fast Bun runtime and the lightweight Hono framework. Learn to set up routing, stream API responses, implement middleware like loggers, render server-side JSX, and perform robust testing. The tutorial also covers crucial topics like input validation with Zod and creating end-to-end type-safe APIs with Hono's built-in RPC client.

chapters.description: This chapter walks through initializing a new project with Bun and integrating the Hono framework to handle HTTP requests.

chapters.description: Learn how to define routes in Hono using an Express-like API, handle requests with the context object, and organize routes into separate files.

chapters.title: The Context Object and API Streaming
chapters.description: Explore the Hono context object's capabilities and see a practical example of how to easily implement HTTP streaming.

chapters.title: Adding Middleware
chapters.description: This chapter covers how to add middleware to your Hono application, using the built-in logger as a practical example.

chapters.title: Server-Side Rendering with JSX
chapters.description: Learn how to use JSX as a templating language for server-side rendering in Hono, including the necessary configuration.

chapters.title: Testing Your Hono API with Bun
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to write and run tests for your Hono API endpoints using Hono's test-helpers and Bun's built-in test runner.

chapters.title: API Input Validation with Zod
chapters.description: Discover how to secure your API by validating incoming request data at the framework layer using Hono's Zod validator middleware.

chapters.title: End-to-End Type Safety with RPC
chapters.description: Explore Hono's RPC feature, which provides end-to-end type safety between your Hono backend and a client application, similar to tRPC.

summary:
## Why Switch from Express.js?

While Express.js is an incredible and foundational framework, it has become outdated and slow compared to modern alternatives. New tools offer better performance, simpler APIs for modern tasks, and improved developer experiences.

## The Hono + Bun Stack

This video advocates for a stack combining **Hono** for the web framework and **Bun** for the JavaScript runtime.

*   **Hono**: A small, simple, and ultra-fast web framework that can run on any JavaScript runtime (Node.js, Deno, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, etc.). Its API will feel familiar to Express developers.
*   **Bun**: An all-in-one JavaScript toolkit and runtime focused on speed and performance. It includes a package manager, test runner, and bundler.

## Getting Started

Setting up a basic server is straightforward:

1.  Initialize a new project: `bun init`
2.  Install Hono: `bun install hono`
3.  Create a Hono app instance and plug it into Bun's native server.

```typescript
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()

app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hello Hono!'))

export default {
  port: 3000,
  fetch: app.fetch,
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> Hono uses a single **Context object (`c`)** in its route handlers, which combines the functionality of Express's `req` and `res` objects for a more convenient API.

## Core Hono Features

### Routing and Middleware

*   **Routing**: Hono provides familiar routing methods like `app.get()`, `app.post()`, etc. You can also group related routes using `app.route('/path', routeHandler)`. 
*   **Middleware**: Hono has full middleware support, both for custom functions and pre-built helpers like the `logger` middleware, which can be imported directly from `hono/logger`.

### Server-Side JSX

Hono allows you to use **JSX as a templating language** for server-side rendering, which is a powerful alternative to systems like EJS.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This feature renders JSX to static HTML on the server. It is not a full-stack React framework like Next.js and does not include client-side JavaScript by default.

### Streaming

The framework provides a simple `c.stream()` API to easily stream responses to the client. This is extremely useful for applications like AI chat UIs that need to incrementally display data.

### Testing

Hono provides built-in testing helpers that integrate seamlessly with **Bun's test runner**. This allows for a simple and efficient way to write API tests without external dependencies like `supertest`.

```typescript
// index.test.ts
import app from './app' // Your exported Hono app

describe('Hello Route', () => {
  it('should return 200 with a message', async () => {
    const res = await app.request('/hello')
    expect(res.status).toBe(200)
    expect(await res.json()).toEqual({ message: 'hello world' })
  })
})
```

### Validation and Type Safety

*   **Validation**: Hono has a rich ecosystem of validation middleware. The `@hono/zod-validator` allows you to validate incoming request bodies, query params, and headers using **Zod schemas**.
*   **RPC (Remote Procedure Call)**: Hono offers a built-in, tRPC-like experience. By defining routes with validators, Hono can infer the API's type signature. You can then use the `hono/client` library on the frontend to make fully type-safe API calls, ensuring end-to-end type safety between your client and server.

## Leaving Express.js for Hono and Bun

I have completely stopped using expressjs and node and I'm going to show you what I'm using Instead. This is Hono and it kind of looks like Express, and this is a good thing. Express did a lot of things right. It's a really incredible framework, it's just become outdated and slow compared to these modern alternatives.

Hono can run on any JavaScript runtime so you can run it on node if you want, but it also runs on things like Lambda and Cloudflare workers and my absolute favorite is bun. It's ultra fast and lightweight. It's only 14 kiloby and it has everything that you would need in a web server. So it handles middleware and testing, and it even lets you write jsx instead of having to use something like ejs. So I'm going to set up a project just to show you how this all works.

## Project Setup: Bun and Hono

Let's make a server folder and I'm going to bun in it a new project for this and let's just open this up in VS Code.

So this is a minimal bun project and we can set up an HTTP server by calling bun.serve and passing in a fetch function. And let's run this on Port 3030 instead and I am going to run this with bnat index.ts. So we got that console log coming out and this is running on Port 3030. So that's how easy it is to set up a server on bun. But now let's add hono to this.

So I'm going to bun install hono and go back here and import hono from hono and it's going to feel a lot like Express. The first thing I do is create a new app and then this just plugs straight into bun server. So instead of putting a custom function here, we're going to pass in app.fetch from hono and now all HTTP requests coming into the bun server are just going to be handled by this framework, which gives us a much nicer API.

## Implementing Basic and Grouped Routes

So let's go back over to hono, let's look at routing real quick and you can see that you get all the route methods that you're already used to. There's tons you can do with all this. I'm just going to set up a basic route for now. So let's go app.get hello, and then instead of Rec res, we get this context object, and then we can use one of the helper methods, so let's return some Json here, hello world and this is all in typescript it's all type safe. Uh, let's see what actually happens now if I go to /hello and we get that JSON response.

And let's go back to hono, and you can see it basically has all the features that you would want from Express, uh, including these groups here. So I'm actually going to copy this example because I think a common thing in Express is to make a routes folder, and then organize your routes in here. So this example has books.ts, uh, and I'm just going to dump this in here. I need to import hono. I create this new router using hono and then I set up a bunch of routes. I should actually export this, so let's export default book. And then in my index TS, I can just import this app.route books book router, perfect. So now if I go back into the browser, I can go to /book and it gives us this text that's coming from the routes over here.

So this API should be really familiar except that instead of Rec res, we now have this context object.

## The Context Object and API Streaming

Let's go back to the documentation. We can see all the things that context gives us here. So all incoming data and outgoing data is handled through this context object and it's a really convenient object to use. We can return JSON, we can return HTML, which is also how we turn JSX. And somewhere down here, yeah, there's a streaming API.

So this one is really cool. I'm just going to copy all of this code here cuz I use this recently to set up a GPT app and stream down the llm response. So I'm just going to set up a loop here and we're going to await stream.write line hello I and then we'll sleep for one second. So if I delete the rest of this code. I'm going to call this uh /stream. We go back into the browser now, we should be able to see an HTTP response being streamed down to the client. So let's see, hello 0, hello 1. And this is working, it streamed all of those down incrementally like you see modern apps doing. And this was so much easier to get working on Hono than it has been on any other framework I've tried using.

## Adding Middleware

Let's look at the next thing here. So there is middleware. Again, this works kind of like Express. We can use custom middleware or we can use some built-in middleware. So actually it's probably pretty handy if we include the logger middleware that we can import straight from Hono. So I'll put that in here and now every time I go to a request, let's should go to /hello, uh, in the logs I should be able to see what's going in, what's going out. So that's kind of nice. Then there's helpers. These are all really awesome, I'll let you check those out.

## Server-Side Rendering with JSX

Then there's JSX. Just imagine if instead of ejs, you got to use JSX as your templating language. So I'm going to pull this example code out here and I'm just going to make a new page, let's call it page.tsx and dump this code in. Uh, and then I need to import hono, uh, and then I get this error because I actually need to change my tsconfig.json settings. So let's go here, tsconfig, jsx, at the comma. And then at the bottom here, I'm going to remove this and instead I'm going to export default, uh, top it looks like this is called. So I'm just exporting the JSX component out of this. And then in my other file, I'm going to import top from page.tsx. I'm going to paste in that code and I think that any file that uses jsx needs to have the extension TSX. But now I've got my normal route set up and then right here when I want to render some HTML, I can use this JSX, which is awesome. So let's just make sure that worked. If I go to the root route here, I get that JSX page rendered.

And this isn't a replacement for something like Next.js or Remix, but it is a really nice lightweight solution and it does support a bunch of react features. Like you can use async components. It does have support for suspense, but it's really just a lightweight layer that is going to render the JSX as HTML and send that down to the client, which means there's also no client side JavaScript here. So if you did need to run react in the browser, you would probably set up a Vite application with your Hono server and have those two work together. And leave me a comment if you want me to make a tutorial on how to do that.

## Testing Your Hono API with Bun

So let's check out testing now because if you've ever tried to test an Express app using super test, and just this is basically the better version of that. So it's all built in already. I can just take one of these examples. Let's go for this one and at the same time, I'm going to open up Bun because I want to take a look at how to write test the bun way. Okay, so I'm going to copy this code example 2, and if I go back in here, I'm going to make a new file index.test.ts, paste in the bun code, but instead of just testing that 2 + 2 equal 4 let's test. Guess I'll import describe and I'll need to import the app. So import app from... actually I'm going to refactor this slightly. So I've got my index file with all of this in it. I'm going to take all of this hono code out and I'm going to make an app.tsx. So this file creates the app, sets up all the routes and then exports the app out of here. Then my index file can import app from app, and this will work just as normal. And then in my test file, I can import that app, perfect. Okay, so this will make it really easy to test that API.

So now I can make a request to, let's see which routes I actually have set up. Let's go for hello. So I'm going to make a request to /hello, and I want to test that the status that comes back is 200, and that the response that comes back, the JSON that comes back is actually hello world. So I can paste that in here, and instead of 2B, I'm pretty sure it has to be to equal. And then I'm going to go back into terminal here and I'm just going to run Bun test. And of course that passes. It was a very simple test but I just wanted to demonstrate how easy it is to start testing your APIs with this framework.

## API Input Validation with Zod

Let's now take a look at validation because this is probably one of the most important things to have on your web server. Users could send any type of data to your API and you need to validate that data before you do anything with it. And we have typescript which works to check our types before our code runs, but we need to make sure we have something in place to check our types as our code is running. So this is a really nice thing to have at the API layer. And down at the bottom, I think they have a Zod validator. Yep. So we have to install this middleware, so I will bun install this. And then I'm just going to copy this code to demo how it works. So back in app, I'm just going to dump in this route here, and I'm going to need to import this validator, paste that in at the top. I also need to make sure that I have Zod installed and I need to import that as well. And then this is complaining because I'm not matching that signature, which is a really good thing. So let's just return something out of here. And then this works in a really similar way as before where I have app.post. I have my route. But now I have this validator middleware in the middle that is going to make sure that the data coming in, I'd actually probably make sure this is JSON data, has to be a JSON object with a body property that is a string, and if this requirement isn't met, then it's going to send an error message down to the client.

## End-to-End Type Safety with RPC

And that leads into the next awesome feature of this which is RPC. So if you did set up something like your react app with your hono app, you can export the type of the route that you create with the validator, and then in your client application you can import that type, import the hono client library, and then you get type safety on your client as well as your server every single time you make an HTTP request. And this works kind of like tRPC, but it's baked into hono. And there's a lot more to explore here, but I'll let you check it out for yourself.
